metaData.originalTitle: 别再迷信 RAG 了！Grep 回归，向量索引沦为备胎？
metaData.title: Stop Idolizing RAG! Grep Makes a Comeback, Vector Indexing Becomes a Fallback?
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article dissects the technical architecture of Claude Code, which abandons RAG and vector indexing in favor of LLM-driven Grep for code search, demonstrating that in code search scenarios, a zero-index Grep approach outperforms traditional embedding retrieval in both efficiency and effectiveness.
metaData.summary: Centered on the core debate of 'Is RAG dead?', this article uses the leaked source code of Claude Code as a starting point to detail its zero-index code search mechanism. It first introduces Claude Code's core search loop: the LLM autonomously decides on a search strategy, using tools like GrepTool, GlobTool, FileReadTool, and AgentTool for iterative searches until sufficient information is gathered. Next, it delves into the performance principles of the underlying tool, ripgrep, including five layers of filtering, SIMD acceleration, and the Boyer-Moore algorithm. Real-world test data shows that for a developer's local project scale, brute-force scanning incurs only millisecond-level latency. The article also compares Claude Code with Cursor (dual-index architecture) and Codex (also zero-index), pointing out that architectural choice depends on data scale: zero-index is suitable for local projects, while indexing is geared towards large codebases. Addressing criticism of the Grep approach's high token cost, the article analyzes Claude Code's three-tier cost control mechanisms: prompt caching, auto-compaction, and sub-agent isolation. Finally, citing academic research (GrepRAG) and experimental data, it argues why exact matching outperforms semantic retrieval in code search, concluding that what is dying is not the RAG paradigm itself, but the default assumption that 'code search must rely on embedding pre-indexing'.

mainPoints.point: Claude Code abandons RAG and vector indexing, adopting an LLM-driven, multi-round Grep search approach.
mainPoints.explanation: Its core search mechanism lets the LLM autonomously decide on search keywords and tools, conducting multiple iterative rounds using Grep, Glob, Read, and other tools until information is sufficient, rather than relying on a pre-built vector index.

mainPoints.point: At the scale of a developer's local project, ripgrep's brute-force scanning performance is sufficient to replace vector retrieval.
mainPoints.explanation: Through optimizations like .gitignore filtering, path restrictions, SIMD acceleration, and multi-threading, ripgrep achieves millisecond-level latency for searching projects with thousands of files, eliminating the need for pre-built indexes.

mainPoints.point: The nature of code search dictates that exact matching (Grep) is superior to semantic retrieval (Embedding).
mainPoints.explanation: Identifiers like function names and class names in code serve as precise semantic anchors; 95% of search keywords are identifiers. Exact matching is more direct and effective than semantic similarity, a finding also confirmed by the GrepRAG paper.

mainPoints.point: Architectural choice depends on data scale; zero-index and dual-index are not a matter of technical superiority.
mainPoints.explanation: Claude Code's zero-index approach is suitable for local projects ranging from MBs to a few hundred MBs, while Cursor's dual-index architecture targets larger codebases. Both are reasonable choices for different scenarios.

mainPoints.point: The token cost of the Grep approach can be effectively managed through mechanisms like prompt caching, auto-compaction, and sub-agent isolation.
mainPoints.explanation: Claude Code significantly reduces the token overhead of multi-round searches by caching repeated prompt prefixes, automatically compressing conversation history, and isolating search tasks within sub-agents.

keyQuotes: It's not that RAG is dead, but the specific way of doing RAG—'pre-building indexes and performing static one-time retrieval'—is being replaced in certain scenarios.
Plain glob and grep, driven by the model, beat everything.

95% of code search keywords are identifiers: class names (36%), method names (41%), and variable names (18%). Identifiers themselves are the semantics of the code; exact matching is the most direct retrieval method.
What is dying is not the paradigm of Retrieval-Augmented Generation, but the default assumption that code search must rely on embedding pre-indexing.
Technology choices are determined by the characteristics and scale of the data, not by matters of faith.
